newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt defends role as Mideast peace mediator.
newsitem.headline: Egypt defends role as Mideast peace mediator.

text.p: President Hosni Mubarak on Wednesday said Egyptian mediation was vital for Middle East peace talks, dismissing Israeli criticism it was biased toward the Palestinians.

PLO officials had said on Tuesday both Israel and the United States -- the main sponsor of the peace process -- were irked by Egypt's input into talks on Israel's long-delayed handover of the West Bank city of Hebron to the Palestinians.
An Israeli official said Cairo's position was biased and "could bring not only a situation of tension but also confrontation with Egypt."
Mubarak, saying Cairo had a central role in starting Arab-Israeli peace talks in 1991, told reporters: "Those who ask about Egypt's role, let them show us what they can do without Egypt."

Egypt, which in 1979 became the first Arab country to make peace with the Jewish state, has brokered many rounds of talks between Israel and the PLO. Palestinian President Yasser Arafat regularly consults with Mubarak.
"Egypt is the peace monger. Egypt instigated the peace process and our presence does not need permission. Egypt's role is there and you cannot live without it," he said.
Mubarak said Israeli envoy Dore Gold would hold talks in Cairo about a future visit by Egypt's Foreign Minister Amr Moussa aimed at advancing the Hebron talks.
But the senior Israeli official, who did not want to be identified, said Gold intended to stop Moussa's visit because he would "only complicate the process."

Israel wants to change terms of its redeployment in Hebron to give more protection to 400 militant Jewish settlers in the heart of the city of 100,000 Arabs. Palestinians refuse any changes to the accord signed by the previous Israeli government.

"They want us to press on (Palestinian President Yasser) Arafat to accept their proposals whether the public opinion in Palestine agreed to it or not or whether Mr. Arafat finds it feasible or not," Mubarak said.
Mubarak, saying Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government had asked Moussa to mediate over Hebron, criticised the Israel comments, which he said reflected Israeli internal politics.
"It's bad after you have discussed something to then go home to Israel and say statements that are against all that you agreed upon," he said.
Relations between Egypt and the Jewish state have been strained since Israelis elected Netanyahu, who rejects peace policies of the former Labour government.

Egypt hosted a pan-Arab summit in June that accused Israel of foot-dragging in the peace process. Mubarak and other Egyptian officials have also lashed out at Netanyahu's aim to increased Jewish settlement on occupied Arab land.

But Mubarak dismissed any chance of a Middle East conflict and brushed aside an Israeli general's warning that Syria would be "clobbered" if it started a war. Syrian-Israel talks are deadlocked, with Netanyahu ruling out a return of the occupied Golan Heights as demanded by Damascus.

"They won't attack Syria or do anything of that sort," he said. "Attacking Syria is very dangerous for the region and for Israel and they (Israel) have said that they don't have the intention to do so. War is an outdated option."
